items.meaning: Your voice is becoming unclear or intermittent during a call due to a poor connection.
items.example: I'm sorry, you're breaking up a bit; could you try repeating that last sentence?
items.plain: I'm sorry, your voice is unclear; could you try repeating that last sentence?
items.note: Common phrase to indicate poor audio quality on a call. Can be said directly.

items.meaning: The speaker's audio is not coming through at all, or is too faint to understand.
items.example: Hello? I can't hear you at all, is your microphone muted perhaps?
items.plain: Hello? Your audio isn't working, is your microphone muted perhaps?
items.note: Direct and common way to state an audio problem. Often followed by a suggestion.

items.meaning: The phone or video call connection quality is poor, causing audio or video issues.
items.example: I think the line is bad today; I keep losing parts of what you're saying.
items.plain: I think the connection is poor today; I keep losing parts of what you're saying.
items.note: A general way to describe a poor connection, often used for phone calls.

items.meaning: Your voice or video is intermittently disappearing and reappearing during the call.
items.example: It sounds like you're cutting out every few seconds, making it hard to follow.
items.plain: It sounds like your voice is disappearing every few seconds, making it hard to follow.
items.note: Similar to "breaking up" but often implies more frequent, shorter interruptions.

items.meaning: The link between your device and the internet, often cited as the cause of call issues.
items.example: I apologize, my internet connection seems unstable, which is why my video keeps freezing.
items.plain: I apologize, my internet seems unstable, which is why my video keeps freezing.
items.note: Used to explain personal technical difficulties. Can be followed by an apology.

items.meaning: A question to confirm if your audio is working and being received by the other person.
items.example: Hello? Can you hear me now? I just switched my microphone.
items.plain: Hello? Is my audio working now? I just switched my microphone.
items.note: Very common opening question on calls, especially when there have been issues.

items.meaning: Used to indicate that another participant has disconnected from the call.
items.example: I think we lost Sarah; she's no longer showing in the participant list.
items.plain: I think Sarah disconnected; she's no longer showing in the participant list.
items.note: A polite way to acknowledge a participant's unexpected departure from a call.

items.meaning: The image on the other person's video feed is not updating or moving.
items.example: Excuse me, your screen is frozen; I can't see you moving at all.
items.plain: Excuse me, your video image is stuck; I can't see you moving at all.
items.note: Direct way to point out a video issue. Can be followed by a suggestion to reconnect.

items.meaning: Expresses an intention to attempt to connect again, usually by phone.
items.example: The video isn't working, so let me try calling you on your mobile instead.
items.plain: The video isn't working, so I will call you on your mobile instead.
items.note: Used when switching communication methods due to technical problems.

items.meaning: Indicates a difficulty or problem with a specific aspect of the call or technology.
items.example: I'm having trouble with my audio settings; can you give me a moment?
items.plain: My audio settings are difficult to manage; can you give me a moment?
items.note: A common, polite way to explain a personal technical delay.

items.meaning: The sound on the call is intermittently stopping and starting, making it hard to hear.
items.example: I'm afraid the audio is cutting in and out, so I'm missing some words.
items.plain: I'm afraid the sound is stopping and starting, so I'm missing some words.
items.note: Describes an intermittent sound issue. Often followed by a request to repeat.

items.meaning: A question to confirm if your video feed is working and visible to the other person.
items.example: My camera light is on, but can you see me clearly on your end?
items.plain: My camera light is on, but is my video visible on your end?
items.note: Common question to check video functionality, especially after joining or fixing issues.

items.meaning: Your voice is becoming faint or unclear, indicating a worsening connection.
items.example: I'm losing you a bit, could you speak up or move closer to your router?
items.plain: Your voice is becoming faint, could you speak up or move closer to your router?
items.note: Similar to "breaking up" but often implies a gradual decline in clarity.

items.meaning: Your camera is not transmitting an image, either intentionally or due to a technical issue.
items.example: I'm sorry, my video is off today as I'm having some bandwidth issues.
items.plain: I'm sorry, my camera is not on today as I'm having some bandwidth issues.
items.note: A direct statement to explain why one's camera is not active.

items.meaning: A polite request for the other person to say something again, usually due to poor audio.
items.example: Sorry, the connection dropped for a second; could you repeat that last part?
items.plain: Sorry, the connection dropped for a second; could you say that last part again?
items.note: Very common and polite way to ask for clarification due to technical issues or misunderstanding.

items.meaning: Used to describe what you perceive about the other person's audio quality or situation.
items.example: It sounds like you're in a noisy place; is it possible to move somewhere quieter?
items.plain: You seem to be in a noisy place; is it possible to move somewhere quieter?
items.note: A gentle way to comment on background noise or audio issues from the other side.

items.meaning: A shared acknowledgment that the call quality is poor for both parties.
items.example: It seems we have a bad connection today; maybe we should try again later.
items.plain: It seems our call quality is poor today; maybe we should try again later.
items.note: Implies a mutual problem, often leading to a suggestion to reschedule or try another method.

items.meaning: States an intention to leave and rejoin the call to fix a technical issue.
items.example: My video is frozen, so I'll try reconnecting to see if that helps.
items.plain: My video is frozen, so I will leave and rejoin to see if that helps.
items.note: Common solution for persistent audio/video problems on video calls.

items.meaning: A question to confirm if your audio input device is active and transmitting sound.
items.example: I'm speaking, but is my microphone on? I don't see the indicator light.
items.plain: I'm speaking, but is my audio input active? I don't see the indicator light.
items.note: Asked when unsure if one's audio is being broadcast, often after joining a call.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask for permission to interrupt and contribute to the conversation.
items.example: Sorry, can I just jump in here with a quick thought on that point?
items.plain: Sorry, may I interrupt here with a quick thought on that point?
items.note: Informal and polite way to interrupt, often used in group discussions.

items.meaning: A polite opening to contribute an additional point or perspective to the discussion.
items.example: If I could just add to what you're saying, I think the timeline is crucial.
items.plain: I'd like to add to what you're saying, I think the timeline is crucial.
items.note: A very polite and slightly formal way to interject a point.

items.meaning: An apology followed by a reason for breaking into someone else's speech.
items.example: Sorry to interrupt but we're running short on time for this agenda item.
items.plain: I apologize for interrupting but we're running short on time for this agenda item.
items.note: Standard polite interruption, often used to manage time or correct information.

items.meaning: A request to be allowed to complete one's thought or argument without interruption.
items.example: Please, let me finish my point before you respond to my proposal.
items.plain: Please, allow me to complete my thought before you respond to my proposal.
items.note: Used when someone is being interrupted and wants to continue speaking. Can be firm.

items.meaning: An invitation for the other person to speak before you, often when both start at once.
items.example: Oh, sorry, we spoke at the same time. Go ahead, you first.
items.plain: Oh, sorry, we spoke at the same time. Please speak before me.
items.note: Common polite phrase when two people start talking simultaneously.

items.text: What were you going to say
items.form: what were you going to say
items.meaning: A question asking someone to continue their interrupted thought or contribution.
items.example: I cut you off earlier; what were you going to say about the budget?
items.plain: I interrupted you earlier; what did you intend to say about the budget?
items.note: Polite way to invite someone to speak after an interruption, acknowledging the interruption.

items.meaning: A formal way to express a desire to interrupt and add a comment or question.
items.example: If I may, I'd like to interject a quick question about the project timeline.
items.plain: If I may, I want to add a quick question about the project timeline.
items.note: More formal than "jump in," suitable for professional settings.

items.meaning: Used to return to a previous topic or point in the conversation.
items.example: To go back to your earlier comment about the client, I have an update.
items.plain: Returning to your earlier comment about the client, I have an update.
items.note: Useful for steering the conversation back to a relevant, previously discussed point.

items.meaning: An invitation for someone to continue speaking after a pause or interruption.
items.example: Sorry for the distraction, John. You were saying about the new policy?
items.plain: Sorry for the distraction, John. Please continue talking about the new policy.
items.note: Common and informal way to prompt someone to resume their speech.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly formal request to join the conversation or offer a point.
items.example: Excuse me, may I come in here for a moment to share some data?
items.plain: Excuse me, may I speak for a moment to share some data?
items.note: Polite and slightly more formal than "can I jump in," suitable for meetings.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a brief, often important, point or clarification.
items.example: Before we move on, I just wanted to say that I agree with your assessment.
items.plain: Before we move on, I want to state that I agree with your assessment.
items.note: A common, slightly informal way to add a quick thought or opinion.

items.meaning: Used to explain something more clearly or correct a potential misunderstanding.
items.example: I think there's a misunderstanding, so let me clarify that point for everyone.
items.plain: I think there's a misunderstanding, so I will explain that point more clearly for everyone.
items.note: Useful for ensuring accuracy and preventing confusion in discussions.

items.meaning: Indicates that you are finished speaking and the other person can resume their turn.
items.example: That's all I wanted to add, so I'll let you continue with your presentation.
items.plain: That's all I wanted to add, so please continue with your presentation.
items.note: Polite way to hand over the speaking turn after making a point.

items.meaning: A question inviting someone to contribute to the discussion, often after a pause.
items.example: We've heard from everyone else, Sarah, did you want to add anything?
items.plain: We've heard from everyone else, Sarah, do you have anything to contribute?
items.note: Polite way to invite participation, ensuring everyone has a chance to speak.

items.meaning: An apology followed by an invitation for the other person to speak first.
items.example: Oh, I'm sorry, you go; I didn't realize you were about to speak.
items.plain: Oh, I apologize, please speak first; I didn't realize you were about to speak.
items.note: Very common and informal phrase when two people start speaking simultaneously.

items.meaning: Used to formally transfer the speaking turn or responsibility to another person.
items.example: Now that I've covered the introduction, I'll hand it over to Mark for the details.
items.plain: Now that I've covered the introduction, Mark will speak about the details.
items.note: Common in presentations or structured meetings to transition speakers.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a final point or question about the current topic before changing it.
items.example: Before we move on to the next agenda item, does anyone have any questions?
items.plain: Before we discuss the next agenda item, does anyone have any questions?
items.note: Useful for ensuring all points on a topic are covered before transitioning.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a brief, concise comment or piece of information.
items.example: Just a quick point on the budget: we need to factor in shipping costs.
items.plain: I have a brief comment on the budget: we need to factor in shipping costs.
items.note: Informal and common way to add a short, relevant piece of information.

items.meaning: A promise to be concise and not speak for too long.
items.example: I know we're short on time, so I'll keep it brief with my update.
items.plain: I know we're short on time, so I will be concise with my update.
items.note: Polite way to signal that your contribution will be short, respecting others' time.

items.meaning: A direct statement indicating that you have finished your contribution and others can speak.
items.example: That's all from me; I'm done speaking on this topic for now.
items.plain: That's all from me; I have finished my contribution on this topic for now.
items.note: Clear and direct way to signal the end of your turn, less common than "that's all."

items.meaning: Used to signal the beginning of the conclusion of a discussion or meeting.
items.example: Okay, to wrap things up, let's quickly review our action items.
items.plain: Okay, to conclude, let's quickly review our action items.
items.note: Very common and informal way to transition to the end of a conversation or meeting.

items.meaning: Suggests ending the work or discussion for the current day.
items.example: We've made good progress, so let's call it a day and pick this up tomorrow.
items.plain: We've made good progress, so let's finish for today and continue this tomorrow.
items.note: Informal and common phrase to suggest ending work or a meeting.

items.text: I think we're out of time
items.form: I think we're out of time
items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that the allotted time for the discussion has expired.
items.example: Unfortunately, I think we're out of time for further discussion on this point.
items.plain: Unfortunately, our time has expired for further discussion on this point.
items.note: Common and polite way to manage meeting time, often used by a facilitator.

items.meaning: A gentle suggestion that it's time to conclude the call or meeting.
items.example: It's almost 5 PM, so we should probably finish up this call soon.
items.plain: It's almost 5 PM, so we need to conclude this call soon.
items.note: Polite and indirect way to suggest ending a conversation.

items.meaning: States an intention to contact someone again later regarding a specific matter.
items.example: I'll follow up with an email summarizing our discussion and action points.
items.plain: I will send a follow-up email summarizing our discussion and action points.
items.note: Very common in professional contexts to confirm next steps or information.

items.meaning: A suggestion to arrange a future conversation to continue a discussion.
items.example: We didn't cover everything, so let's schedule another call for next week.
items.plain: We didn't cover everything, so we should arrange another call for next week.
items.note: Common way to plan continuation of a discussion that couldn't be finished.

items.meaning: A polite expression of gratitude at the end of a meeting or conversation.
items.example: Well, thanks for your time today; I found our discussion very productive.
items.plain: Well, I appreciate the time you spent today; I found our discussion very productive.
items.note: Standard polite closing, especially in professional or semi-formal contexts.

items.meaning: A polite and friendly closing remark, expressing enjoyment of the conversation.
items.example: I really enjoyed catching up; it was good to talk with you again.
items.plain: I really enjoyed catching up; I liked talking with you again.
items.note: Common, friendly closing, suitable for both personal and professional calls.

items.meaning: States an intention to communicate information or a summary via email.
items.example: To confirm the details, I'll send an email with all the relevant documents.
items.plain: To confirm the details, I will email you all the relevant documents.
items.note: Common way to promise written follow-up after a verbal discussion.

items.meaning: Indicates that all necessary topics or points have been discussed.
items.example: I think we've covered everything on the agenda, so we can conclude.
items.plain: I think we have discussed all topics on the agenda, so we can conclude.
items.note: Used to signal readiness to end a meeting or discussion.

items.meaning: An informal way to say you need to leave the call or meeting.
items.example: Apologies, but I need to jump off for another meeting in five minutes.
items.plain: Apologies, but I need to leave this call for another meeting in five minutes.
items.note: Informal and common, especially in video calls, to politely excuse oneself.

items.meaning: A promise to contact the other person again in the near future.
items.example: Thanks for the update; I'll be in touch next week with our decision.
items.plain: Thanks for the update; I will contact you next week with our decision.
items.note: Common closing, indicating future communication, can be formal or informal.

items.meaning: A suggestion to reconnect briefly in the near future to discuss progress or updates.
items.example: We've made a plan, so let's touch base soon to review the initial results.
items.plain: We've made a plan, so let's talk briefly soon to review the initial results.
items.note: Common in professional settings for informal follow-up meetings or calls.

items.meaning: A promise to respond or provide information at a later time.
items.example: I don't have that information right now, but I'll get back to you by end of day.
items.plain: I don't have that information right now, but I will respond to you by end of day.
items.note: Very common phrase for promising a future response, often with a timeframe.

items.meaning: A question to check if there are any remaining topics or questions before concluding.
items.example: Before we finish, is there anything else we need to discuss today?
items.plain: Before we finish, do we need to discuss anything else today?
items.note: Common closing question in meetings to ensure all points are covered.

items.meaning: A statement indicating that you have finished your contribution or the discussion is complete.
items.example: From my side, I think that's all for today's update.
items.plain: From my side, I believe my update is complete for today.
items.note: Informal and common way to signal the end of one's turn or the meeting.

items.meaning: An informal, friendly farewell, wishing the other person a good day, evening, etc.
items.example: Alright, I'll talk to you later then. Have a good one!
items.plain: Alright, I'll talk to you later then. Have a good day!
items.note: Very common, informal, and versatile farewell.

items.meaning: Expresses anticipation for a future meeting, call, or interaction.
items.example: Thanks for the productive discussion; looking forward to our next meeting.
items.plain: Thanks for the productive discussion; I anticipate our next meeting.
items.note: Polite and common closing, especially in professional contexts, to maintain rapport.

items.meaning: States an intention to transmit a summary or record of the discussion.
items.example: I'll send over the notes from our call by the end of the day.
items.plain: I will transmit the notes from our call by the end of the day.
items.note: Common in professional settings to ensure everyone has a record of decisions.

items.meaning: Suggests continuing the discussion or task at a later time or date.
items.example: We're out of time now, but we can pick this up again tomorrow morning.
items.plain: We're out of time now, but we can continue this discussion again tomorrow morning.
items.note: Common and informal way to postpone a discussion or task.

items.meaning: An instruction on an answering machine or voicemail to record a message after a signal.
items.example: You've reached my voicemail; please leave a message after the tone.
items.plain: You've reached my voicemail; please record a message after the tone.
items.note: Standard phrase heard on voicemail greetings.

items.meaning: A promise to return a phone call at a later, more convenient time.
items.example: I'm in a meeting right now, but I'll call you back in about an hour.
items.plain: I'm in a meeting right now, but I will return your call in about an hour.
items.note: Very common and direct way to promise to return a call.

items.meaning: A request on voicemail for the caller to identify themselves.
items.example: When you hear the beep, please leave your name and number.
items.plain: When you hear the beep, please state your name and number.
items.note: Standard request on voicemail greetings.

items.meaning: A statement indicating that you were unable to answer a phone call.
items.example: Sorry, I missed your call earlier; I was in a meeting.
items.plain: Sorry, I didn't answer your call earlier; I was in a meeting.
items.note: Common and polite way to acknowledge a missed call when returning it or messaging.

items.meaning: States that you are calling back someone who previously called you.
items.example: Hi Sarah, I'm returning your call about the project update.
items.plain: Hi Sarah, I am calling you back about the project update.
items.note: Standard opening phrase when calling someone back.

items.meaning: A polite request for the other person to return your phone call.
items.example: I'm having connection issues, so could you call me back on my landline?
items.plain: I'm having connection issues, so please call me back on my landline.
items.note: Polite and common way to ask for a return call, often with a reason.

items.meaning: An informal promise to send a short message, usually an email or text.
items.example: I'll drop you a line later today with the meeting agenda.
items.plain: I will send you a short message later today with the meeting agenda.
items.note: Informal and friendly way to say you'll send a message.

items.meaning: States an intention to send a short message via mobile phone.
items.example: I'm running late, so I'll send you a text when I'm five minutes away.
items.plain: I'm running late, so I will send you a message when I'm five minutes away.
items.note: Direct and common way to promise a text message.

items.meaning: States an intention to send specific information via email.
items.example: I don't have the full report here, but I'll email you the details this afternoon.
items.plain: I don't have the full report here, but I will send you the details by email this afternoon.
items.note: Common in professional contexts for providing information in writing.

items.meaning: A statement indicating that you cannot take a call or engage in conversation immediately.
items.example: My apologies, I'm not available right now, please leave a message.
items.plain: My apologies, I cannot speak right now, please leave a message.
items.note: Standard phrase for voicemail greetings or when declining a call.

items.meaning: A request on voicemail for the caller to provide comprehensive information.
items.example: I'm away from my desk; please leave a detailed message and I'll get back to you.
items.plain: I'm away from my desk; please record a comprehensive message and I'll get back to you.
items.note: Common on professional voicemail greetings to get necessary information.

items.meaning: A promise to contact someone very soon.
items.example: Thanks for your inquiry; I'll be in touch shortly with a response.
items.plain: Thanks for your inquiry; I will contact you very soon with a response.
items.note: Polite and professional way to indicate a quick follow-up.

items.meaning: An informal promise to call someone on the phone.
items.example: I'll check my calendar and then I'll give you a ring to confirm our meeting.
items.plain: I'll check my calendar and then I will call you to confirm our meeting.
items.note: Informal and friendly way to say "I'll call you."

items.meaning: A promise to contact someone, often in a professional context, by any means.
items.example: I'll gather the information and then I'll reach out to you next week.
items.plain: I'll gather the information and then I will contact you next week.
items.note: Common in professional settings, more formal than "get in touch."

items.meaning: A promise to contact someone, usually by phone or email.
items.example: I'll review the proposal and then I'll get in touch with my feedback.
items.plain: I'll review the proposal and then I will contact you with my feedback.
items.note: Common and versatile phrase for promising future communication.

items.meaning: States an intention to check the status or progress of a specific item.
items.example: I'll follow up on that request with the team and let you know.
items.plain: I will check the status of that request with the team and let you know.
items.note: Common in professional settings for tracking tasks or information.

items.meaning: States an intention to review voicemails, texts, or emails.
items.example: I'm not sure if I received it, but I'll check my messages after this call.
items.plain: I'm not sure if I received it, but I will review my messages after this call.
items.note: Common phrase when unsure about receiving a communication.

items.meaning: A promise to reply to a message or inquiry without delay once a condition is met.
items.example: I'll respond as soon as I have all the necessary information from the team.
items.plain: I will reply once I have all the necessary information from the team.
items.note: Polite and professional way to manage expectations about response time.

items.text: I'll get back to you on
items.form: I'll get back to you on
items.meaning: A promise to provide a response or information about a specific topic later.
items.example: I don't have the figures now, but I'll get back to you on the budget details.
items.plain: I don't have the figures now, but I will provide you with the budget details later.
items.note: Similar to "I'll get back to you" but specifies the topic.

items.meaning: A question to confirm if the other person is still connected and listening, often after a pause.
items.example: Hello? Are you still there? I haven't heard anything for a moment.
items.plain: Hello? Are you still connected? I haven't heard anything for a moment.
items.note: Common question when there's silence or a suspected connection issue on a call.

items.meaning: Experiencing problems with the internet or phone signal that affect call quality.
items.example: I'm having connection issues, so my video might be a bit unstable today.
items.plain: My internet is unstable, so my video might be a bit unstable today.
items.note: A common and direct way to explain technical difficulties during a call.

items.meaning: A question to check if your audio is understandable without distortion or interruptions.
items.example: I just switched headsets, can you hear me clearly now?
items.plain: I just switched headsets, is my audio understandable now?
items.note: More specific than 'Can you hear me?', asking about clarity.

items.meaning: Your microphone is turned off, preventing others from hearing you.
items.example: Oops, sorry, my audio is muted; I was talking to myself!
items.plain: Oops, sorry, my microphone is off; I was talking to myself!
items.note: Common self-correction when realizing you've been speaking unheard.

items.meaning: A polite way to indicate that a participant has disconnected from the call.
items.example: We seem to have lost David; perhaps his internet dropped out.
items.plain: David appears to have disconnected; perhaps his internet dropped out.
items.note: Slightly more formal than 'I think we lost', often used in meetings.

items.meaning: A polite request for the other person to talk louder.
items.example: It's a bit noisy here, could you speak up a little, please?
items.plain: It's a bit noisy here, could you talk louder, please?
items.note: Common request when the other person's volume is too low.

items.meaning: Experiencing general problems with equipment or software during the call.
items.example: Please bear with me, I'm having technical difficulties with my camera.
items.plain: Please bear with me, my camera is not working correctly.
items.note: A general and polite way to explain any technical problem.

items.meaning: States an intention to review and adjust audio or video configurations.
items.example: I can't hear you, let me check my settings quickly.
items.plain: I can't hear you, I will quickly review my settings.
items.note: Common response when troubleshooting personal audio/video issues.

items.meaning: Hearing your own voice or other sounds repeated back during the call.
items.example: I'm getting an echo on my end; could you check your microphone?
items.plain: I hear a repeated sound on my end; could you check your microphone?
items.note: Common problem on calls, often caused by an open microphone or speaker.

items.meaning: A question to confirm if your shared screen content is visible to others.
items.example: I'm sharing the presentation now, can you see my screen?
items.plain: I'm sharing the presentation now, is my screen visible?
items.note: Essential question when starting a screen share in a video call.

items.meaning: States an intention to turn off your microphone to avoid background noise.
items.example: There's some background noise here, so I'll just mute myself for a moment.
items.plain: There's some background noise here, so I will turn off my microphone for a moment.
items.note: Polite way to manage audio quality, especially in group calls.

items.meaning: An apology for unintentionally interrupting someone by talking at the same time.
items.example: Oh, sorry, I spoke over you there; please continue with your point.
items.plain: Oh, I apologize, I interrupted you there; please continue with your point.
items.note: Common and polite apology for accidental interruption.

items.meaning: A polite request to be allowed to complete your current thought or sentence.
items.example: If you don't mind, let me just finish this sentence, then I'll hear your thoughts.
items.plain: If you don't mind, allow me to complete this sentence, then I'll hear your thoughts.
items.note: Used when you are being interrupted and want to conclude your statement.

items.meaning: Used to introduce a question about a specific topic.
items.example: Before we move on, I wanted to ask about the next steps for the project.
items.plain: Before we move on, I had a question about the next steps for the project.
items.note: Common way to introduce a question, often after someone else has spoken.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask for permission to make a brief statement or comment.
items.example: Could I just say that I completely agree with your last point?
items.plain: May I briefly state that I completely agree with your last point?
items.note: Polite and slightly informal way to interject a quick opinion.

items.meaning: Indicates that you are giving the other person the opportunity to speak or lead.
items.example: I've finished my part, so I'll let you take over the discussion now.
items.plain: I've finished my part, so you can lead the discussion now.
items.note: Common in meetings to transition leadership or speaking turns.

items.meaning: Used to re-explain something you said to ensure it is understood correctly.
items.example: To clarify my point, I meant we should prioritize quality over speed.
items.plain: To explain my idea more clearly, I meant we should prioritize quality over speed.
items.note: Useful for rephrasing or adding detail to a previous statement.

items.meaning: A promise to provide new information as it becomes available.
items.example: I'll check on that for you and I'll keep you updated on the progress.
items.plain: I'll check on that for you and I will inform you of any new progress.
items.note: Common in professional and personal contexts for ongoing situations.

items.meaning: A suggestion to bring the current discussion or meeting to a close.
items.example: We're almost at time, so let's wrap this up with a summary of decisions.
items.plain: We're almost at time, so let's conclude with a summary of decisions.
items.note: Informal and direct way to suggest ending a conversation or meeting.

items.meaning: States an intention to ensure something is dispatched, usually by email.
items.example: Thanks for the information; I'll get that sent to the team right away.
items.plain: Thanks for the information; I will ensure it is sent to the team right away.
items.note: Common in professional settings for confirming action on a document or email.

items.meaning: Indicates that there is not much time left for the discussion or meeting.
items.example: We're running short on time, so let's quickly go through the last points.
items.plain: We have little time left, so let's quickly go through the last points.
items.note: Common phrase to manage time in a meeting, often used by a facilitator.

items.meaning: A promise to contact the other person in the near future.
items.example: I'll review the documents and I'll be in touch soon with my feedback.
items.plain: I'll review the documents and I will contact you soon with my feedback.
items.note: Common and polite closing, indicating future communication without a specific date.

items.meaning: A promise to phone someone.
items.example: I'll check my schedule and then I'll give you a call to arrange a meeting.
items.plain: I'll check my schedule and then I will phone you to arrange a meeting.
items.note: Common and direct way to promise a phone call.

items.meaning: States an intention to provide current information or progress report.
items.example: I'll check the status of your order and I'll send you an update by email.
items.plain: I'll check the status of your order and I will email you a progress report.
items.note: Common in customer service or project management for providing information.

items.text: I'll get back to my desk
items.form: I'll get back to my desk
items.meaning: States an intention to return to one's workspace, often to retrieve information.
items.example: I don't have that file here, but I'll get back to my desk and send it to you.
items.plain: I don't have that file here, but I will return to my desk and send it to you.
items.note: Common phrase when needing to access resources from one's office.

items.meaning: An informal promise to send an email.
items.example: I'll confirm the details and then I'll drop you an email with the summary.
items.plain: I'll confirm the details and then I will send you an email with the summary.
items.note: Informal and friendly way to say you'll send an email.

items.meaning: States the time or date when you will be free to communicate or meet.
items.example: I'm in meetings until noon, but I'll be available from 1 PM onwards.
items.plain: I'm in meetings until noon, but I will be free from 1 PM onwards.
items.note: Useful for setting expectations about your availability.

items.meaning: States an intention to send an electronic invitation for a meeting.
items.example: Let's schedule that for next week; I'll send a calendar invite shortly.
items.plain: Let's schedule that for next week; I will send an electronic meeting invitation shortly.
items.note: Common in professional settings for formalizing meeting arrangements.

items.meaning: A promise to contact a specific person or department.
items.example: I'll get in touch with the sales team regarding your query.
items.plain: I will contact the sales team regarding your query.
items.note: Common in professional settings when referring a query to another party.

items.meaning: A promise to phone someone at a subsequent, unspecified time.
items.example: I'm busy right now, but I'll call you later this afternoon.
items.plain: I'm busy right now, but I will phone you later this afternoon.
items.note: Common and informal way to postpone a call.

items.meaning: States an intention to transmit a web address or meeting invitation.
items.example: I'll send you the link for the video call right before it starts.
items.plain: I will transmit the web address for the video call right before it starts.
items.note: Common for sharing access to online meetings or resources.

items.meaning: A promise to return very quickly after a brief absence.
items.example: Excuse me for a moment, I'll be right back; I just need to grab a drink.
items.plain: Excuse me for a moment, I will return very quickly; I just need to grab a drink.
items.note: Common phrase when stepping away briefly from a call or meeting.

items.meaning: States an intention to temporarily pause the call, usually to find information.
items.example: I need to check something, so I'll put you on hold for a minute.
items.plain: I need to check something, so I will temporarily pause the call for a minute.
items.note: Standard phrase used by customer service or receptionists on phone calls.

items.text: I'll get back to my emails
items.form: I'll get back to my emails
items.meaning: States an intention to resume checking and responding to emails.
items.example: I've finished the call, so I'll get back to my emails now.
items.plain: I've finished the call, so I will resume checking and responding to my emails now.
items.note: Common phrase to indicate a return to email correspondence after a call.

items.meaning: A promise to inform someone about something at a later time.
items.example: I'll confirm the details with my manager and I'll let you know by tomorrow.
items.plain: I'll confirm the details with my manager and I will inform you by tomorrow.
items.note: Very common and versatile phrase for promising future information.

items.meaning: States an intention to send a subsequent message or email to reiterate points.
items.example: Thanks for the discussion; I'll send a follow-up email with the action points.
items.plain: Thanks for the discussion; I will send a subsequent email with the action points.
items.note: Common in professional settings to summarize or confirm after a meeting.

items.meaning: States that you will be occupied with a meeting at a specific time.
items.example: I can't take calls then, as I'll be in a meeting all morning.
items.plain: I can't take calls then, as I will be occupied with a meeting all morning.
items.note: Common way to explain unavailability, often on voicemail or in messages.

items.meaning: A promise to return a phone call immediately or very soon.
items.example: I'm just stepping out for a second, but I'll call you right back.
items.plain: I'm just stepping out for a second, but I will return your call immediately.
items.note: More urgent than 'I'll call you back', implying a very short delay.

items.meaning: States an intention to obtain specific data or facts.
items.example: I don't have that to hand, but I'll get the information and send it over.
items.plain: I don't have that to hand, but I will obtain the information and send it over.
items.note: Common in professional contexts when needing to retrieve data.

items.meaning: States that you will not be at your workplace and likely unavailable.
items.example: I'll be out of office next week, so please contact my colleague.
items.plain: I will not be at my workplace next week, so please contact my colleague.
items.note: Standard phrase for automatic email replies or informing colleagues.

items.meaning: A promise to transmit a communication, usually by text or email.
items.example: I'll confirm the time and I'll send you a message later today.
items.plain: I'll confirm the time and I will transmit a communication later today.
items.note: General phrase for promising to send a written communication.

items.meaning: A promise to re-establish communication after a period of silence.
items.example: I'll review your proposal and I'll be back in touch by the end of the week.
items.plain: I'll review your proposal and I will contact you again by the end of the week.
items.note: Common closing, implying a future follow-up after a task is completed.

i'll follow up with.note: Checker slip: The key accurately describes the intention to communicate further regarding a specific matter.
